scenes.visual: Title card 'Tap, Drain and a Sensor' over a charcoal silhouette of a young cockerel beside a schematic tank. COLOUR MAP for both films: secretion (gland tap) ORANGE; hormone level (water line in the plasma tank) TEAL; clearance (drain: every way the body removes or breaks down the hormone) GREY; negative feedback = RED dashed arrow from the level back to the tap. Animals charcoal silhouettes, named on screen.

scenes.tts: What can an organ send through the body without any nerves? And what decides how much of it is in the blood? A physician in Göttingen asked the first question with young cockerels.
scenes.visual: A young cockerel silhouette, label 'young cockerel'. A nerve bundle beside it is snipped by scissors; a question mark hovers over the bird. Caption 'Arnold Berthold, Göttingen, published 1849'.
scenes.narration: What can an organ send through the body without any nerves? And what decides how much of it is in the blood? A physician in Göttingen asked the first question with young cockerels.

scenes.tts: He castrated them. Without testes, the birds grew small combs, and they crowed little. In some birds he put a testis back into the belly. It was cut off from its original nerves. Those birds still grew combs and crowed.
scenes.visual: Two cockerels grow side by side over time. Left, label 'castrated': stays small-combed. Right: an ORANGE blob labelled 'testis graft' appears in the belly with a cut nerve stub (crossed-out line); its comb grows and a speech-bubble 'crow' appears.
scenes.narration: He castrated them. Without testes, the birds grew small combs, and they crowed little. In some birds he put a testis back into the belly. It was cut off from its original nerves. Those birds still grew combs and crowed.

scenes.tts: So the graft must have sent something through the blood. That something is a hormone. A hormone is a chemical released by one group of cells into the blood. The blood carries it to distant cells. Only cells with a receptor for it respond.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the graft. ORANGE dots leave it into a red-brown blood vessel and flow past four cells. Only the two cells with a cup-shaped 'receptor' catch dots and light up; the other two stay dark. Label 'hormone' on the dots.
scenes.narration: So the graft must have sent something through the blood. That something is a hormone. A hormone is a chemical released by one group of cells into the blood. The blood carries it to distant cells. Only cells with a receptor for it respond.

scenes.tts: Now picture the blood as a tank. The gland is a tap, pouring hormone in. A drain stands for every way the body removes or breaks down the hormone. The water line is the hormone's level in the blood. It settles where what drains out matches what pours in.
scenes.visual: A clear tank labelled 'plasma (schematic)'. ORANGE tap at top labelled 'gland: secretion'. GREY drain at the bottom labelled 'clearance: all removal and breakdown'. Tap opens; TEAL line rises; the outflow stream from the drain thickens as the line rises. Two arrows, 'in' and 'out', grow until equal length; the line flattens, label 'in = out'.
scenes.narration: Now picture the blood as a tank. The gland is a tap, pouring hormone in. A drain stands for every way the body removes or breaks down the hormone. The water line is the hormone's level in the blood. It settles where what drains out matches what pours in.

scenes.tts: In tank terms, castration shut a tap, and the male traits faded. The graft opened a tap again, and the traits came back. Berthold never measured the hormone itself.
scenes.visual: Same tank, tagged 'model'. A small castrated-cockerel icon beside it. The ORANGE tap closes; the TEAL line drains toward the bottom; the bird's comb shrinks. The graft icon slides onto the tap, which reopens; the comb regrows and a 'crow' bubble returns. The TEAL line is drawn dashed, with the tag 'level not measured by Berthold'.
scenes.narration: In tank terms, castration shut a tap, and the male traits faded. The graft opened a tap again, and the traits came back. Berthold never measured the hormone itself.

scenes.tts: In mammals, one tap can drive another. Take the human stress axis. The hypothalamus releases C R H. Short veins called portal vessels carry it straight to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then releases A C T H. And A C T H makes the adrenal cortex release cortisol.
scenes.caption: In mammals, one tap can drive another. Take the human stress axis. The hypothalamus releases CRH. Short veins called portal vessels carry it straight to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then releases ACTH. And ACTH makes the adrenal cortex release cortisol.
scenes.visual: Label 'adult human'. Three ORANGE taps stacked down the screen: 'hypothalamus: CRH', 'anterior pituitary: ACTH', 'adrenal cortex: cortisol'. A short vessel labelled 'portal vessels' joins the first two. As each tap flows, its stream turns the next tap's handle open. The last tap pours into the cortisol tank with its TEAL line and GREY drain.
scenes.narration: In mammals, one tap can drive another. Take the human stress axis. The hypothalamus releases CRH. Short veins called portal vessels carry it straight to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then releases ACTH. And ACTH makes the adrenal cortex release cortisol.

scenes.tts: Now add a sensor. Cortisol acts back on the hypothalamus and the pituitary, turning their taps down. When cortisol rises, the drive to make it falls. When it drops, the drive rises. This is negative feedback, a response that opposes the change that caused it.
scenes.visual: A RED dashed arrow curves from the TEAL cortisol line up to the CRH and ACTH taps. The line rises; the red arrow brightens; both taps narrow; the line eases back. Then the line dips; the arrow fades; the taps widen; the line recovers. Label 'negative feedback'.
scenes.narration: Now add a sensor. Cortisol acts back on the hypothalamus and the pituitary, turning their taps down. When cortisol rises, the drive to make it falls. When it drops, the drive rises. This is negative feedback, a response that opposes the change that caused it.

scenes.tts: Suppose the adrenal glands are removed. Cortisol falls, because nothing secretes it. What happens to A C T H?
scenes.caption: Suppose the adrenal glands are removed. Cortisol falls, because nothing secretes it. What happens to ACTH?
scenes.visual: The adrenal tap greys out with a cross, label 'adrenals removed'. The TEAL cortisol line drains low. Question card: 'ACTH: up, down or the same?'
scenes.narration: Suppose the adrenal glands are removed. Cortisol falls, because nothing secretes it. What happens to ACTH?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: A C T H rises. With no cortisol feeding back, a key brake is gone. The hypothalamus and pituitary drive harder, but no adrenal can answer. Taking a gland away shows how the rest of the loop responds.
scenes.caption: ACTH rises. With no cortisol feeding back, a key brake is gone. The hypothalamus and pituitary drive harder, but no adrenal can answer. Taking a gland away shows how the rest of the loop responds.
scenes.visual: The RED dashed arrow fades to nothing. The CRH and ACTH taps open wider; the ACTH stream thickens, labels 'CRH up' and 'ACTH up'. It pours onto the crossed-out adrenal tap, which cannot answer.
scenes.narration: ACTH rises. With no cortisol feeding back, a key brake is gone. The hypothalamus and pituitary drive harder, but no adrenal can answer. Taking a gland away shows how the rest of the loop responds.

scenes.tts: Feedback does not freeze the level at one value. In humans, cortisol rises and falls over the day. It also comes in pulses, roughly every sixty to ninety minutes. Feedback adjusts the tap. It shapes a pattern rather than fixing a number.
scenes.visual: The intact loop returns. Beside the tank, a TEAL trace on a 24-hour axis labelled 'schematic': a broad daily wave with small ripples on it. The ORANGE tap flickers in time with the ripples; the RED arrow stays active. Label 'pulses about every 60 to 90 min'.
scenes.narration: Feedback does not freeze the level at one value. In humans, cortisol rises and falls over the day. It also comes in pulses, roughly every sixty to ninety minutes. Feedback adjusts the tap. It shapes a pattern rather than fixing a number.

scenes.tts: So a hormone's level is a balance of secretion in and clearance out. Feedback works on the secretion. How fast the level can follow is a question about the drain.
scenes.visual: Pull back to one tank: ORANGE tap with the RED dashed arrow, TEAL line, GREY drain. The GREY drain pulses gently with a stopwatch icon beside it.
scenes.narration: So a hormone's level is a balance of secretion in and clearance out. Feedback works on the secretion. How fast the level can follow is a question about the drain.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. Take-home line: 'A hormone level balances secretion against clearance; feedback adjusts secretion.'
